Nested Conditional Statements

The one idea to landA nested if asks a second question only after the first one said yes. An elif asks the next question only after the previous one said no. A question that is never reached is never even asked — and indentation is how you write down which is which.

📎

Warm-Up Poll — retrieval on session 10

Warm-Up Poll — three from last session

Recap · Last Session

Quick Check

What does this print?

if 2 > 3:
    print("Conditional Block")
print("End")
  • Conditional Block
  • End
  • both lines
  • nothing

2 — End. Two is not greater than three, so the indented line is skipped. The last line is outside the if, so it always runs.

And this one?

if True:
    print("If Block")
        print("Inside If")
  • both lines
  • If Block only
  • an IndentationError
  • a NameError

3 — IndentationError: unexpected indent. The second print is indented further than the first for no reason. Python will not guess what you meant.

And this?

if False:
    print("If Block")
print("After If")
else:
    print("Else Block")
  • After If, then Else Block
  • After If only
  • a SyntaxError, nothing prints
  • an IndentationError

3 — SyntaxError, and nothing prints at all. A statement between the if and the else breaks the shape, so Python never starts running the file. Not one line.

Instructor — how to run this
  • Signal, announced once: fingers for the option, closed fist for unsure, everyone on "three".
  • 25 seconds a question. Read, vote, press Reveal answer, next.
  • No discussion — this beat buys pace, not depth.
  • Never name a student.
  • Q3 is the one that matters: it is the same parse-time failure they meet again at slide 10.

Behind the Scenes

Instructor — how to run this
  • Ask it as a real question, hands not names: what did the app check, and in what order?
  • Press the button, then stop talking — the gate shuts and the balance check greys out on its own.
  • Say it: a wrong PIN means nobody ever found out whether you had the money.
  • Press again for the turn. The two checks become two indents. r replays it.
  • Call it "an if inside an if", never "two ifs" — that phrase means the wrong shape later.

Agenda — Slide 3

Slide 3Agenda — Nested Conditions -> Else If
  • Two topics on the slide. Say they are one question asked twice.
  • Nested asks the second thing only if the first was true. Else-if, only if it was false.
  • Point at "Indentation" and say it is the notation, not the topic.
  • This is where the one idea gets said. Not at the takeaways.

Concept — The nested shape · Slide 4

Slide 4Nested Conditions — the shape and its three names
  • Ask before you show it: which of these four blocks depends on condition A?
  • If A is false, Python jumps the whole orange box without reading a line of it.
  • That box is the conditional block. Block 2, indented under the inner if, is the nested conditional block.
  • Write 2, 1, 0 on the board — yeses needed for Block 2, Block 3, Block 4.
  • Hand out the worksheet at the end of this slide, not earlier.

Trace It First

Read it. Do not type it yet.

condition_a = True
condition_b = True

if condition_a:
    print("Block 1")
    if condition_b:
        print("Block 2")
    print("Block 3")
print("Block 4")

Two names on top, then the nested if. Those two names are all that will change.

Worksheet task 1. Trace all four combinations on paper and write what each one prints.

Pens only. Four rows, four answers, before any keyboard.

Now type it into the playground and run all four. Change only line 1 and line 2.

Tick the rows you got right. Circle the ones you got wrong.

Instructor — how to run this
  • Code on the wall, nothing running. Four rows on paper first — the keyboard settles the argument, it does not make it.
  • Short of time: they still trace all four on paper, but run only rows 3 and 4.
  • While they trace, say nothing. While they type, watch only for print("Block 2") indented twice.
  • Share-out: which two rows printed the same, and what does that say about condition B?
  • Rows 3 and 4 match. When A is false, B is never read, so its value cannot show in the output.

Hands-on 2 — Nesting inside else

Hands-on 2 — Nesting inside else

Nested Conditions

Nesting Inside Else

Compare this with the program you just ran. What is different?

condition_a = False
condition_b = True

if condition_a:
    print("Block 1")
else:
    if condition_b:
        print("Block 2")
    print("Block 3")
print("Block 4")

Hands up. Do not type anything yet.

Now type it — I am typing it too, keep pace with me. Predict the output, run it, then try other values of condition_a and condition_b.

condition_a = False
condition_b = True

if condition_a:
    print("Block 1")
else:
    if condition_b:
        print("Block 2")
    print("Block 3")
print("Block 4")

a False, b True -> 2, 3, 4 · a False, b False -> 3, 4 · a True, either b -> 1, 4. When a is True the whole else is skipped, so b is never read at all.

Instructor — how to run this
  • Ask for the difference first. Take hands until someone says the inner if moved into the else.
  • Then type it together — you on the projector, them on their machines, same pace.
  • Predict before every run.
  • Then let them change both names freely and report which blocks never printed.
  • The point: when condition_a is True the else is skipped entirely, so condition_b is never read.

Instructor — how to run this
  • Trace the first two lines aloud together, saying what the machine does before what the line means.
  • Then they trace it alone. Short of time: skip the pairing, go from silent work to the live run.
  • Take the verdict: does it work? Yes — it prints 9, which is correct.
  • Then they type it with line 9 at the far left — the faulty version — and run both inputs.
  • Ask why one input errors and the other does not. That is the payoff, and slide 5 is the code.
Answer key
InputCorrect codeAfter the line is moved to column 0
5 2 1prints 5prints 5, then NameError
1 2 9prints 9prints 9, cleanly

The same broken program is right for one input and dead for the other. That is why an indentation bug survives testing — and they made it themselves, so nobody can say it was a trick.

Discover it first — how would you grade this?

Discover it first — how would you grade this?

Conditional Statements

Your Turn

I have a student's marks out of 100 and I need to print their grade.

91 to 100   ->   A
 81 to 90   ->   B
 71 to 80   ->   C
 61 to 70   ->   D

How would you write that with what you know so far? Three minutes. Paper or screen, your choice.

You already have everything you need. There is no new keyword yet.

Two shapes came back. One is shorter. One is correct. Neither is both.

Four separate ifs

if marks >= 91:
    print("A")
if marks >= 81:
    print("B")
if marks >= 71:
    print("C")
if marks >= 61:
    print("D")

Short and flat — and wrong. 95 marks prints A, B, C and D, because every question still gets asked after a match.

An if inside an if inside an if

if marks >= 91:
    print("A")
else:
    if marks >= 81:
        print("B")
    else:
        if marks >= 71:
            ...

Correct — and four levels deep. Add one more grade and it goes deeper again.

You want the second one's behaviour with the first one's shape: ask the next question only if the last said no, without indenting further each time. Python has one word for that.

Instructor — how to run this
  • Put the four bands up and ask the question. Do not mention elif.
  • Three minutes, quiet. Walk the rows and look at what they write.
  • You will see two shapes: a run of separate ifs, and a deep nest. Both work.
  • Take one of each on the board, then ask what is wrong with each.
  • Do not correct either one. The next slide is the answer to the problem they just felt.
📘

Concept — elif, the answer · Slides 7–9

Slide 7Elif Statement — the skeleton
  • One new keyword. Elif means: if the previous question was false, here is the next one.
  • No box inside a box. All three questions sit at the same indent.
  • Say it out loud: this is a ladder, not a nest.
Slide 8Elif — A True, the whole tail is unreachable
  • Second vote of the session. Vote, argue with a neighbour, vote again, then reveal.
  • The question: A is true and B is true — how many conditions does Python test?
  • Answer: one. No label on B, because there is nothing to label.
  • If A were false it would ask B, and the moment a rung fires the ladder stops.
Slide 9Multiple Elif Statements — the grade ladder
  • This is their problem, solved. Same four bands, one rung each.
  • Ask for the output before anything else. Marks are 72 — what prints?
  • C. Three conditions tested; 61 and the else were never looked at.
  • Chain as many elifs as you like, and the final else is optional — leave it off and 40 marks prints nothing.
  • Break it: move the 61 check to the top. Now 72 gets D, and the code is still perfectly valid.
✏️

Two Programs

Two programs, one word different on line four. For every condition write whether Python tested it — yes or no. Not true or false.

   Program P                Program Q
1  a = 5                 1  a = 5
2  if a > 3:             2  if a > 3:
3      print("X")        3      print("X")
4  if a > 1:             4  elif a > 1:

Both conditions are true in both programs, of the same variable.

Instructor — how to run this
  • Fill P's first two rows aloud, then 90 seconds alone on both tables.
  • Third vote round: "does Program Q print a Y?" Vote, argue 45 seconds, vote again, then reveal.
  • Reveal one row at a time so they find their own divergence point.
  • Then: hands up if your Q table has a Y in it. Four-second diagnosis, anonymous.
  • Short of time: trace P only and say what Q prints.

Hands-on — Add one more grade

Hands-on — Add one more grade

Multiple Elif Statements

Add One More Grade

Type the ladder from the slide. Run it with a few different marks and check every grade comes out right.

marks = 72

if marks >= 91:
    print("A")
elif marks >= 81:
    print("B")
elif marks >= 71:
    print("C")
elif marks >= 61:
    print("D")
else:
    print("F")

95, 85, 72, 65, 40 should give A, B, C, D, F.

I have forgotten grade E, for 51 to 60. Add it to your program — put it at the bottom, after the else.

else:
    print("F")
elif marks >= 51:
    print("E")

Run it. What happened?

SyntaxError: invalid syntax — and nothing printed at all. Not even the grades that worked a minute ago. Python read the whole file, found a rung after the catch-all, and refused to start.

So where does grade E belong? Move it and get all six grades working.

Test 95, 85, 72, 65, 55, 40. You should get A, B, C, D, E, F.

Instructor — how to run this
  • They type the ladder from slide 9 and check a few marks. 3 min.
  • Then ask for grade E, 51 to 60 — after the else. Do not warn them; let them run it and react.
  • Short of time: move E yourself instead of letting them find where it goes.
  • The surprise is that nothing prints. They expect the earlier grades to still work.
  • Then: where does E belong? They move it above the else and test all six.
Answer key

After the else: SyntaxError: invalid syntax, nothing runs. Correct place: a fourth elif marks >= 51 above the else. Then 95, 85, 72, 65, 55, 40 give A, B, C, D, E, F.

📘

Concept — Why that failed · Slide 10

Slide 10Common Mistake — elif after else
  • This is what they just hit with grade E. Put it up as the confirmation, not the reveal.
  • Else has to be last, because else means everything remaining — and nothing remains after that.
  • Name the error out loud: SyntaxError, and not one line of the file runs.
  • Same family as poll Q3. Slide 5 ran and then broke; this one never started. Tell those two apart and you can debug.
📘

Slides 11–12 — The problem, then they solve it

Slide 11Question — divisible by 10 or by 5 or neither
  • N modulo five equals zero is how you ask "does five divide this".
  • Take the number ten. Divisible by ten? Yes. By five? Also yes.
  • Let that sit for five seconds without resolving it. The next beat is built on it.
Slide 12Output format — then they solve it
  • Read the second rule slowly: "if divisible by five, but not ten", and the three strings character for character.
  • Then hand it over: five minutes, their machines, no help from you. Walk the rows and say nothing.
  • Anyone who used three separate ifs — run 10 on their screen and let them watch two lines print.
  • Then write it yourself on the projector, naming each rung — and leave it up, the next beat edits it.
  • Short of time: cut the solve to three minutes and start writing it sooner.
💻

Hands-on 3 — Order matters

Hands-on 3 — Order matters

If - Elif - Else

Order Matters

You have a working program. Now swap the rungs: make divisible by 5 the if, and divisible by 10 the elif. Nothing else changes.

Predict first. Then run 25, 30, 9 and 10.

25 and 9 are still right. But 30 and 10 both print Divisible by 5. Every multiple of ten is now wrong, and the rung for ten can never be reached — the looser rule catches the number first. The program is still perfectly valid Python.

Instructor — how to run this
  • They already have a working program on screen. This is one edit, not a rewrite.
  • Predictions out loud before any run.
  • 25 and 9 still pass. Only the multiples of ten break — a test would not have caught it.
  • Ask what happened to the rung for ten. It is now unreachable.
  • Say it: with elif, the order you write the rungs in is part of the answer.
Answer key
InputCorrect orderRungs swapped
25Divisible by 5Divisible by 5
30Divisible by 10Divisible by 5
10Divisible by 10Divisible by 5
9Not Divisible by 10 or 5Not Divisible by 10 or 5

Instructor — how to run this
  • Code and stem up. Bottom of page 3, nobody collects it, and the full stop is printed there for a reason.
  • Hard floor: whatever is unfinished elsewhere, stop it and start this. 90 seconds writing.
  • Take three out loud, volunteers only. Write two up word for word, including a half-answer.

Full: "...pin_ok was false, so Python never reached the balance check."  Half: "Because the PIN was wrong." Anything naming never reached, inside or never asked is there.

Instructor guide

1 · The one idea

A nested if asks its second question only if the first said yes. An elif asks the next question only if the previous said no. A question that is never reached is never asked.

Say it at slide 3. Ask for it back at slide 13.

2 · Before you walk in

  • Print the worksheet — three pages, single-sided, one each. The Student worksheet button prints the sheets only.
  • Open the code playground. Font sized for the back row, line numbers on.
  • Presenter view, then f for full screen. a all slides · g guides · r replay · Esc out. If full screen refuses, you are in a preview pane — open the file in its own browser tab.
  • Two typing blocks are real time: nine lines in Hands-on 1, and they write the divisible program themselves after slide 12. Do not plan around them being faster.
  • Never cut: the hook · the grade-ladder discovery · slide 8's vote · the indentation break · the grade E discovery · the swap · the exit sentence.

3 · If they ask

  • Is elif the same as else if? Same behaviour. elif is one keyword at the if's indent; C, Java and JS have no elif, so their else if is a nested if the formatting hides. Neither is the correct one.
  • How many nested ifs am I allowed? No limit you will hit, but flatten past about three. A smell, not an error.
  • So AI is just a big if-else? No. A network computes weighted sums, no branch. A decision tree branches, but learns its own order. Today a person chooses the order — that is the part that goes wrong.
  • Should I always write an else? Contested. Optional; leaving it out means "do nothing", which is sometimes right and sometimes a bug that prints nothing and looks like success.
  • Why not just use and? Often you should. Nesting earns it when the two failures need different responses, or the second question is unsafe to ask first.
